units: the inner circulation of the tree starts up again at the end of the cold season
the nourishing liquid climbs from the root system toward the top of the tree
the pressure gap between waterlogged ground and dry air drives that climb
a very thin living tissue under the protective layer of the trunk carries this liquid
the growth organs open and release a folded blade
during the warm season the foliage makes sugary reserves
the tree stores these reserves in its trunk and its roots
in the season of falling leaves the foliage loses its green coloring
through the cold season the tree keeps a faint breathing
the cycle repeats only if the base of the trunk stays healthy and water keeps coming
text: When the cold finally loosens its grip, a tree sets to work where nobody can see it. Sap climbs out of the roots and up toward the highest branches, driven by the gap in pressure between soaked ground and the dry air above. Just under the bark, a thin sleeve of living cells carries that sweet flow upward. One by one the buds swell, split open, and let out a leaf folded tight like a fan. Through the warm months those leaves manufacture sugars, and the tree banks them away in its trunk and its roots. Come the season of falling leaves, the green drains out of them and they let go. Winter looks like sleep, yet the tree still breathes, faintly, living off what it put by. The whole round begins again as long as the base of the trunk stays sound and the roots find water deep enough down.

units: someone the narrator knows told him about an incident in his hedge
he had seen a round opening dug under a shrub
he closed that opening with a slab of rock to drive off a small mammal
the leaves of the shrub yellowed about two weeks after it was blocked
the underground tunnel was in fact draining rain water away
closing it turned the base of the hedge into a hollow where water stood
the roots, cut off from air, wasted away
he took the slab off and dug a channel to carry the water out
the shrub got its vigor back the following season
text: An acquaintance of mine described what went wrong in his hedge, and the story has stayed with me ever since. He had found a neat round hole dug under one of the shrubs, so he laid a flat slab of rock over it to drive off the small animal he blamed for it. About two weeks later, the leaves on that shrub yellowed and curled. The tunnel, it turned out, had been draining the place: rainwater vanished down into it. Once the mouth was plugged, the ground under the hedge became a shallow basin, water stagnated there, and the roots suffocated for want of air. He removed the slab again and excavated a channel to carry the water away. By the next growing season the shrub had all its strength back. He regards holes differently now, wondering what the animal had worked out about that soil long before he did.

units: a sharp drop in temperature at the end of the cold season can destroy an orchard crop in one night
ice crystals damage the open blossom and the new shoots
watching the sky in the evening is advised, to judge the danger
no cloud and no wind are signs of high risk
watering the ground moderately before the temperature falls helps it hold heat
wrapping the vulnerable trunks in a breathable cloth, without tightening it, is recommended
no cutting at all should be done on the branches at this time
any cut makes a wound that the cold makes worse
at sunrise the frosted branches should be sprayed with lukewarm water, little by little
writing the episode down is advised, to keep the memory of the seasons
text: A hard freeze late in the cold season can wipe out an orchard crop overnight, since the ice burns the open blossom and the shoots that have just come out. Here is how to hold the damage down. Look at the sky first, in the evening: no cloud and no wind, and the danger is high. Water the ground lightly before the temperature falls, because damp earth takes heat in and gives it back through the night. Wrap the trunks that are most at risk in a cloth that breathes, loosely, so the air can still move around them. Cut nothing at all in this stretch of the year, since every cut leaves behind a wound that the cold will make worse. At sunrise, spray the frosted branches with lukewarm water, little by little. Then write the whole episode down, so the memory of the seasons is not lost.

units: one side of the valley is covered with dense forest growth
there you find a bed of rotting plant matter and a smell of organic soil
the opposite side still carries the marks of felling done long ago
on that bare side the stone shows and water cuts grooves in it
the thin grassy cover there does not hold the nourishing layer
a member of staff in charge of the sector takes visitors from one side to the other
she explains that under the trees water sinks into the ground instead of running off the surface
the water point at the bottom of the valley is still flowing at the end of the hot season
gradual planting has been started on the stripped side, with species whose roots spread wide
the result will not be visible for several decades
text: On one side of the valley the forest has closed over everything: close-packed trunks, a deep bed of rotting leaves, a smell of damp earth that clings to your fingers. The far slope still carries the scars of the felling carried out there long ago. Bare stone shows through, rainfall gouges grooves down it, and the thin grass cannot keep the fertile layer in place. A warden who looks after the sector escorts visitors from the one side across to the other. Under the trees, she says, water sinks straight in instead of running off, and the spring at the foot of the valley is still flowing at the end of the hot season. On the stripped slope, replanting has begun, shrub by shrub, with species chosen for roots that spread wide. What comes of it will not show for several decades yet.

units: the outermost layer is thin and greasy and limits water loss
the middle layer holds lime salts and provides the strength
the inner layer, more pliable, serves as an anchor for the muscles
plates set across the back keep the organs out of harm
the jointed segments of the rear part allow the animal to curl up
the joints of the limbs bend in one direction only
sensing hairs lodged in fine pits pick up movement in the water around it
the drawback of this casing is that it cannot get any bigger
the animal must leave its casing from time to time and wait for the new one to harden
through this fragile period it hides under a stone
text: A crustacean's shell reads like a suit of armor put together piece by piece. Its outermost layer is thin and waxy, and it keeps the water inside from escaping. Underneath lies a stiffer layer, saturated with lime salts, which gives the whole casing its strength. A third layer, more pliable, lines the inside and gives the muscles something to pull against. Plates across the back shield the organs. The jointed rings of the tail let the animal curl in on itself. The legs bend on hinges that work one way only. Fine sensory hairs, set in minute pits, pick up every stir in the water around it. All of this carries one flaw: it cannot grow. Every so often the animal has to climb out of its own casing and wait for the replacement to harden. While it is still soft, it hides itself away beneath a stone.

units: the writer finds the lack of response to the retreat of pollinating insects unacceptable
the first warnings sat in field observations that were ignored some thirty years ago
successive counts then established a steady fall in numbers
fruit growers saw that the fertilizing grains were spreading badly
orchards had to fall back on artificial fertilization, costly and unreliable
the writer holds that the burden of proof should change hands
he demands that harmful practice prove it does no damage
strips of flowers along the edge of a plot are named as a cheap remedy
keeping hedges and mowing less often are among the solutions put forward
text: Nothing excuses how little has been done about the retreat of the insects that carry pollen. The first warnings sat there in field notes taken a generation ago, and nobody judged them worth reading. Then came the counts, one after another, each of them showing fewer insects than the one before. Then the fruit growers saw that pollen was no longer traveling as it should, and that their orchards had to be pollinated by hand, an expensive procedure, and an unreliable one. We have reached the point where the burden of proof should change hands. It is not for naturalists to prove the danger, it is for harmful practice to prove that it does no harm. A strip of flowers along the edge of a plot costs next to nothing. Nor does leaving a hedge standing, or mowing the grass less often.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman who runs a place producing young trees had no plans for that trade
she was studying the chemical make-up of soils
a disease striking the young plants of her area changed her path
the seedlings were dying with no visible cause
her examination of the roots turned up a parasitic organism tied to too much watering
she urged watering less often, even at the cost of losing the weakest stock
the growers doubted her at first, then applied her advice
the death rate among the young plants dropped by fifty percent
she was given a nursery to run and set up full tracking of every batch there
she now passes her experience on to beginners
text: The woman who runs a nursery for forest trees had never intended to end up in that trade at all. She was studying the chemistry of soils when a disease swept through the young trees of her district, and that turned her whole path around. Seedlings were dying with nothing visible to account for it, so she dug up the roots and identified a fungus that flourished wherever the watering ran too generous. Her recommendation was blunt: water less often, and accept the loss of the weakest stock. The growers doubted her at first, then did as she said, and mortality among the young trees fell by half. That success earned her a nursery of her own to manage, where she set up a record for every batch, from the seed to the planting out. These days she passes on what she knows to beginners.

units: the narrator was let down by her first visit to an observation trail
the signs gave nothing but scientific names, without saying what to look at
a remarkable pond was hidden by tall growth and was not signposted
she came back after the trail had been overhauled
half the signs have been replaced by questions
an opening has been cleared toward the pond
a low seat has been put in for watching the young water insects
the trail now teaches you to spot the traces animals leave
what is missing is a shortened route suited to families with a stroller
text: My first walk along that observation trail was a genuine disappointment. The signs listed scientific names one after another and never once told you where to put your eyes. A fine pond lay a few steps off the path, hidden away behind a curtain of tall reeds, and nothing pointed to it. I went back once the whole trail had been rebuilt. Half the signs are gone, replaced by questions. An opening has been cleared through toward the pond. A low bench has been installed there, so that you can watch the young insects dart about under the surface. And the trail teaches you at last to read what the animals leave behind, the tuft caught on a thorn, the flattened grass, the bark scraped raw. What it still lacks is a shorter loop, with no steps and no loose gravel, for families pushing a stroller.

units: the writer of the letter writes from her garden to a friend
she compares two planted areas she had already spoken about
the area higher up gets sun from dawn to dusk
the soil there dries out fast and the stems are short and thick
the flowers in the upper area open early and wilt within seven days
the lower area is sheltered by a wall and gets no sun before midday
the plants in the lower area are taller and flower twice as long
the gap comes mainly from how much water the soil holds, since watering and feeding are the same
a rose bush moved from the dry area to the damp one doubled in size in one season
she invites her friend to come before the cold arrives
text: Dear friend, I am writing from the far end of the garden to describe those two beds I mentioned to you. The upper one takes the sun from first light until it goes down again. The soil there dries out quickly, the stems come up short and thickset, and the flowers open early but wither within a week. The lower bed sits against a wall and sees no sun at all before midday. Everything there grows taller and more tender, and the flowering there lasts roughly twice as long. The difference comes down to how much water the ground holds, since I water the two beds in exactly the same way and feed them with the same compost. I moved a rose bush from the dry bed over to the damp one, and it doubled in size within a single season. Come and see the difference for yourself before the cold weather arrives.

units: the renewal of the body covering is presented as a rebuild and not a simple abandonment
in the snake the old casing comes away in a single piece
the snake's eyes go cloudy before this change
the snake rubs against a rough surface to start the tear
in birds the replacement goes part by part, so that the power of flight is kept
the light new plumage grows under the old one and pushes it out
in insects the young stage breaks down almost entirely to form a winged adult
a damaged casing no longer offers protection
an old casing does not adjust to a gain in size
worn plumage gives poor shelter from the cold
text: What is going on when an animal leaves its old skin behind? Molting is not a costume dropped on the floor, it is a rebuild from the ground up. A snake sheds its covering in a single piece. Its eyes cloud over first, and then it rubs itself against something rough to start the tear. A bird renews its covering one feather at a time, so that the power of flight is never lost, and the fresh down grows in underneath until the old feather drops away. In an insect the change goes further still, the young stage breaking down almost entirely and putting itself back together as a winged adult. Why go to such trouble? Because a damaged casing no longer protects, because an old one will not stretch to fit a body that keeps on growing, and because worn feathers hold in hardly any warmth at all.
